The proportion of Ki67-positive cells in the BP-Gel group was comparable to that in the GelMA and control groups, indicating that chondrocyte proliferation was not significantly affected in either hydrogel environment (Fig. R1-2-1; Fig. S1i-j in manuscript).
Figure R1-2-1 Ki67 staining of chondrocytes in different hydrogels. (A) Ki-67 (green)/DAPI (blue) staining of chondrocytes cultured in control, GelMA, and BP-Gel at days 1, 4, and 7. (B) Quantification of Ki-67-positive cells showing comparable proliferation among groups.
(2) Cell counting, analysis of the DNA content, and CCK-8 quantification
To further assess proliferation, we performed cell counting and DNA quantification at Day 7 and CCK-8 assays at Days 1, 4, and 7 in the control (standard medium), GelMA, and BP-Gel groups. Day-7 cell counts and DNA content were comparable across groups, while CCK-8 showed a time-dependent increase with similar proliferation rates among the three groups. These results indicate that the BP-Gel microenvironment supports chondrocyte viability and growth without compromising proliferative capacity (Fig. R1-2-2; Fig. S1k-m in manuscript).
Figure R1-2-2 Cell counting and DNA content at Day 7, and CCK-8 assays at Days 1, 4, and 7 for chondrocytes cultured in control, GelMA, and BP-Gel groups.
(3) Updated the Live/Dead assay figures
To address the reviewer’s concern regarding image quality, we have now updated the Live/Dead assay figures with higher-resolution images and added nuclear staining using Hoechst 33342 (Fig. R1-3; Fig. S1h in manuscript). While DAPI is commonly used for nuclear staining, it is impermeable to live cell membranes and therefore unsuitable for labeling nuclei in live cells. For this reason, nuclear staining was not included in our initial experiments. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we referred to the relevant literature6 and selected Hoechst 33342, which penetrates live cell membranes and enables effective nuclear visualization. This update enables better assessment of cell morphology and density.
Figure R1-2-3 Live/Dead staining of chondrocytes cultured in control, GelMA, and BP-Gel at days 1, 4, and 7.
We believe that these enhancements provide a more robust and scientifically valid demonstration of chondrocyte viability and proliferation within the BP-Gel.
3. Since fibronectin binds to ECM rather than mediates cell-to-cell interactions, further experiments are required to demonstrate chondrocyte intercellular adhesion. Moreover, upregulated gene expression (the authors used RT-qPCR to measure the fn1 and lmn expression) does not necessarily translate to protein function or activity.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. We agree that while Fibronectin-1 (FN1) and Laminin (LAMA) primarily contribute to ECM-cell adhesion, it does not directly mediate intercellular junctions. We also acknowledge that mRNA expression alone cannot fully confirm functional protein activity or cell-cell adhesion. To address this concern and directly evaluate intercellular adhesion between chondrocytes, we conducted the following additional experiments:
(1) Expression of genes related to intercellular adhesion genes
We fully agree with the reviewer that assessing cell aggregation solely based on FN1 and LAMA is not comprehensive. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted a literature survey and selected two representative markers of intercellular adhesion and gap junctions in chondrocytes: N-cadherin (CDH2) and Connexin-43 (GJA1)7-9. These two well-established markers mediate direct cell-cell adhesion and are critical in chondrogenesis and mesenchymal condensation. Accordingly, we performed PCR experiments targeting these genes to preliminarily validate the conclusions from our earlier analyses (Fig. R1-3-1; Fig. S4d in manuscript).
Figure R1-3-1 Expression levels of adhesion-associated genes in chondrocytes after 3 days of culture under different conditions. 2D culture refers to chondrocytes cultured on ordinary plates.
(2) Western blotting analysis of adhesion-related proteins
To assess adhesion protein expression at the protein level, we performed Western blot analysis of four markers: LAMA and FN1 (ECM-mediated adhesion) and CDH2 and GJA1 (intercellular adhesion) in chondrocytes cultured under 2D control, BP-Gel, and GelMA conditions. Protein expression was higher in both GelMA and BP-Gel groups compared with the control, indicating that 3D culture promotes enhanced cell aggregation and stronger intercellular adhesion. Notably, although s GelMA permitted limited proliferation and low-level aggregation, cell activity remained constrained. In contrast, BP-Gel fostered stronger cell–cell interactions, accompanied by markedly higher expression of adhesion-related genes (Fig. R1-3-2; Fig. S4e-f in manuscript).
Figure R1-3-2 Western blot analysis of adhesion-related proteins in chondrocytes cultured under different conditions.
(3) IF staining for adhesion-related proteins
In addition to protein quantification, we examined the spatial distribution of adhesion-related proteins by IF staining using GelMA, BP-Gel, and cell spheroids. Cell spheroids were included as a positive control, as they naturally exhibit high levels of intercellular adhesion. Chondrocytes in the BP-Gel group showed markedly stronger expression of LAMA and FN1 (ECM-mediated adhesion) as well as CDH2 and GJA1 (intercellular adhesion) compared with GelMA, reaching levels comparable to cell spheroids. This indicates that BP-Gel provides an adaptive environment that enhances intercellular connectivity. By contrast, cells in GelMA were restricted by its rigid matrix, showing only localized clusters with limited aggregation, a condition unfavorable for cartilage development (Fig. R1-3-3; Fig. S4g-h in manuscript).
Figure R1-3-3 IF analysis of adhesion-related proteins in engineered chondrocyte tissues. (A) Representative H&E and fluorescence microscopy images illustrating the expression of LAMA1, FN1, CDH2, and GJA1 in chondrocytes cultured with GelMA, BP-Gel, or in cell spheroid form. (B) Quantification of mean gray values for LAMA1, FN1, CDH2, and GJA1 expression.
The corresponding paragraph in the Results section has been revised accordingly:
Page 7, Line 28: “We subsequently evaluated the expression of adhesion-related genes (Lama, Fn1, Cdh2, and Gja1) (Fig. S4d) and cartilage-related genes (Acan, Col2a1, and Sox9) (Fig. 2d). The results showed that the expression levels of these genes in chondrocytes grown in BP-Gel were significantly up-regulated compared with those cultured on plates or in GelMA, indicating that culturing chondrocytes in BP-Gel promotes their aggregation and fusion, thus facilitating cartilage formation. Consistently, Western blotting confirmed higher levels of adhesion-related proteins in the BP-Gel group, and Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and IF staining further demonstrated markedly stronger expression of Laminin subunit alpha-1 (LAMA1), Fibronectin (FN1), N-cadherin (CDH2), and Connexin-43 (GJA1), with quantitative analysis showing significant increases in all four markers (Fig. S4e-h).”
We thank the reviewer again for pointing out this important detail.
4. In Figure 2d, the authors suggest that culturing chondrocytes in BP-gel promotes cellular aggregation and fusion based on chondrocyte-related gene expression data; however, this conclusion lacks adequate support: while Sox-9 and its target Col2 are critical for chondrocyte differentiation, they are not directly implicated in cell adhesion mechanisms and cannot serve as a measure of aggregation and fusion.
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment. We agree that the expression of SOX9 and COL2A1 (Col2), which are indicators of chondrogenic differentiation, are insufficient to assess chondrocyte aggregation or fusion; importantly, we did not intend to use chondrogenic gene expression alone as evidence of these processes. In our manuscript, however, we addressed this issue in two parts. First, we demonstrated that BP-Gel promotes chondrocyte clustering, which is supported by both our original data and the newly supplemented results. Second, we examined cartilage tissues formed under this growth model and compared them with chondrocytes cultured in other hydrogels (GelMA). This comparison was intended to show that the aggregation and fusion behaviors of chondrocytes are beneficial for chondrogenic differentiation, extracellular matrix secretion, and cartilage tissue formation.
(1) Time-lapse confocal imaging of chondrocyte aggregation and fusion
We performed live-cell confocal microscopy to monitor chondrocyte behavior in BP-Gel over 7 days. The time-lapse sequences clearly show small chondrocyte clusters migrating toward each other and fusing into larger aggregates within BP-Gel. This process was not observed in GelMA. Representative images and videos are provided in Fig. R1-4-1 (Fig. 2a-b in manuscript) and Fig. R1-4-2 (Movie S2 in manuscript), respectively.
Figure R1-4-1 Chondrocyte clustering and aggregation in BP-Gel versus GelMA. (A) Growth state of chondrocytes in BP-Gel and GelMA over culture time. The cells were observed under a bright-field microscope. (B) Quantitative analysis of the number of chondrocyte clusters in BP-Gel and GelMA.
Figure R1-4-2 Spontaneous formation of chondrocyte clusters in BP-Gel. (This is an animated GIF. Please view it in a word file or refer to Movie S2)
(2) Cluster fusion and cortical-medullary structure formation
In BP-Gel, small chondrocyte clusters progressively fused into larger aggregates with increasing collagen deposition and cortical thickening, ultimately forming a distinct cortex–medulla architecture over 4 weeks (Fig. R1-4-3; Fig. 2g and 2m-o in manuscript). In contrast, chondrocytes in GelMA remained dispersed without evident fusion (Fig. 2a-b and 2h in manuscript), highlighting the superior ability of BP-Gel to drive cluster fusion and organized cartilage formation.
Figure R1-4-3 Fusion of chondrocyte clusters and cortex-medulla architecture formation in BP-Gel.. (A) Representative micrographs showing the fusion process of chondrocyte clusters in BP-Gel. (B-D) Polarizing microscope images of SR staining tissue specimens collected from different groups at designated time points, and quantitative analysis of intersphere angle of chondrocyte clusters, fluorescence intensity and thickness of cortex layer.
(3) IF staining for chondrogenic markers (SOX9 and COL2A1)
We performed IF staining for SOX9 and COL2A1, using GelMA as a control and including cell spheroids as a reference (Fig. R1-4-4; Fig. S5e-h in manuscript). The results clearly showed that chondrocytes in the BP-Gel group exhibited markedly stronger SOX9 and COL2A1 staining, reflecting both the initiation of chondrogenic lineage differentiation and the enhancement of type II collagen deposition. These findings, together with previous results, demonstrate that BP-Gel promotes intercellular connectivity while supporting cartilage development and maturation.
Figure R1-4-4 IF analysis of chondrogenic markers in cartilage tissues. (A) Representative fluorescence microscopy images of COL2A1 (red) and SOX9 (green) expression in chondrocytes cultured with GelMA, BP-Gel, or as cell spheroids. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). (B) Quantification of SOX9 and COL2A1 mean gray values and SOX9-positive cell ratio.
These data provide comprehensive and multi-angle support for the claim that BP-Gel promotes chondrocyte aggregation and cluster fusion. We have revised the original paragraph and updated the relevant figure legends.
Page 7, Line 10: “Bright-field and confocal microscopy confirmed that chondrocytes aggregated into clusters in BP-Gel, whereas they remained scattered in GelMA (Fig. 2a and Fig. S4a). Quantitative analysis further confirmed that the number of chondrocyte clusters in BP-Gel was significantly greater than that in GelMA at all observation points (Fig. 2b).”
Page 8, Line 21: “Building on these findings, we performed additional IF staining of chondrogenic markers using GelMA as a control and cell spheroids as a reference. Chondrocytes cultured in BP-Gel showed markedly stronger SOX9 and COL2A1 expression than those in GelMA, with quantification confirming higher SOX9 and COL2A1 levels and an increased proportion of SOX9-positive cells (Fig. S5e-h).”
Page 9, Line 4: “Fig. 2g shows a typical fusion process where small chondrocyte clusters fused into a larger chondrocyte cluster.”
Page 10, Line 2: “As shown in Fig. 2m-o, SR staining of BioC at different growth stages revealed progressive fusion of chondrocyte clusters, continuous increase in COL2A1 deposition, and gradual thickening of the cortical layer, reflecting the dynamic formation of a “cortex-medulla” structure.”
The revised version now references functional imaging, protein-level adhesion markers, and blockade validation, rather than relying solely on gene expression of SOX9 and COL2A1. We thank the reviewer again for helping us improve the rigor and clarity of this key conclusion.
5. The comparison of chondrocyte cartilage matrix production in BP-gel (Figure S3h) should include native tissue controls to validate the authors' conclusions.
Reply:
Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that including native cartilage as a benchmark is essential for validating the biomimetic quality of BioC. In the original manuscript, we already compared the morphology and biochemical composition of cartilage-like tissues formed after in vivo implantation with native cartilage (Fig. 2h), showing that the morphology and biochemical composition of BioC closely resembled those of native tissue.
The in vitro developmental stages were presented mainly to highlight that BP-Gel–engineered cartilage undergoes maturation processes similar to natural cartilage development. However, because immature engineered cartilage at early in vitro stages is inherently different from fully mature native cartilage, a direct comparison was not meaningful and thus not included. To address the reviewer’s concern, we have now incorporated histological sections from embryonic mice tracheal cartilage as an additional control group in our histological and biochemical analyses.
(1) Comparison of mature engineered cartilage with native mature cartilage
In the current manuscript, we have already compared mature engineered cartilage with native rabbit tracheal cartilage using identical staining protocols. After 4 weeks of in vivo culture, BioC formed in BP-Gel exhibited cartilage-specific ECM deposition, confirmed by Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), Alcian Blue-Nuclear Fast Red (AB&NFR), and COL2A1 immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (Fig. R1-5-1A; Fig. 2h in manuscript). Quantitative analysis showed that lacunar size in the BP-Gel group was comparable to that of native cartilage. DNA and hydroxyproline measurements further indicated that BioC shared similar biochemical properties with native cartilage (Fig. R1-5-1B-D; Fig. 2i-k in manuscript). Moreover, Sirius Red (SR) staining and 3D reconstruction revealed a grid-like collagen fiber distribution in BioC, closely resembling native tissue, whereas this organization was absent in GelMA (Fig. R1-5-1E; Fig. 2l in manuscript).
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that BioC effectively recapitulates the structural and biochemical features of native cartilage.
Figure R1-5-1 Comparison of engineered cartilage with native tracheal cartilage. (A) Representative H&E, AB&NFR, and COL2A1 IHC staining micrographs of tissue specimens collected from different groups at 4 weeks post-implantation. (B) Quantitative analysis of the size of cartilage lacuna. (C-D) Quantitative analysis of DNA and hydroxyproline content of tissue specimens collected from different groups at 4 weeks post-implantation. (E) Representative SR-stained micrographs of tissue specimens collected from different groups at 4 weeks post-implantation.
(2) Recapitulation of early cartilage development in BP-Gel constructs
At 2 weeks, BP-Gel samples displayed features reminiscent of embryonic cartilage, including tightly aggregated chondrocytes within nascent lacunae and early COL2A1 deposition, whereas GelMA constructs showed delayed organization and minimal matrix formation (Fig. R1-5-2A; Fig. S6a in manuscript). To further clarify this early chondrogenic process, we compared 2-week BP-Gel samples with embryonic tracheal cartilage as a developmental benchmark. Histological staining (H&E, AB&NFR, Safranin O–Fast Green, and SOX9 IF) of mice embryonic trachea at E12.5, E14.5, and E16.5 revealed mesenchymal condensation and early matrix deposition, providing a reference for native chondrogenesis (Fig. R1-5-2B; Fig. S6b in manuscript).
Figure R1-5-2 Early chondrogenic features in BP-Gel constructs compared with embryonic cartilage development. (A) H&E staining of engineered cartilage formed in GelMA and BP-Gel after 2 and 4 weeks in vitro. (B) Histological analyses of mice embryonic trachea at E12.5, E14.5, and E16.5 using H&E, AB&NFR, SO&FG, and SOX9 IF staining.
These additional native-tissue comparisons further confirm that BP-Gel supports the formation of cartilage histologically comparable to native tracheal cartilage. We thank the reviewer again for this valuable suggestion, which has greatly strengthened the rigor of our analysis.
6. The manuscript lacks clear descriptions of the statistical analyses performed across different evaluations, sometimes ANOVA is specified to be used for just 2 groups. Additionally, in multiple instances, the p-value legends in figures do not correspond to what is displayed in the associated graphs (ex. What are the significance numbers for ##, ###,#### in Fig.2o, Fig.3b etc.), please recheck the figures.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this important feedback on statistical analysis and figure annotations.
In the Statistical Analysis section, we previously stated: “For comparisons between two groups, an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. For comparisons among three or more groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test was applied. In cases involving two variables across multiple groups, two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni correction was employed.”
Following the reviewer’s comment, we carefully rechecked all figure legends to ensure ANOVA was not incorrectly applied to two-group comparisons and revised the descriptions accordingly. We have also specified the exact statistical method used in each figure legend. For example:
Page 12, Line 21: “Data in (b) and (r) were analyzed by two-tailed Student’s t-test. Data in (d), (i), (j), (k), (n),and (o) were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s post hoc test.”
Regarding the p-value legends, we thank the reviewer for noting inconsistencies such as the use of “##”, “###”, and “####” in earlier versions of Figures 2o and 3b. These symbols were originally used to distinguish two datasets within the same figure, but we did not clearly indicate this in the legends. All “#” markers have now been removed and replaced with the standardized “*” system across all figures. Statistical significance is consistently denoted as: *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001; ****P < 0.0001. We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important issue.
7. Regarding the in vivo model (Figure 5), the authors' rationale for not using standard tracheal epithelial markers such as KRT5 and p63 remains unclear. The absence of definitive epithelial markers to delineate the epithelium from submucosa complicates interpretation. Furthermore, the authors should address whether the accumulation of K14+ layers in the BP-Gel + IL+Gel condition indicates a squamous phenotype. The substantial variation in replicate numbers across panels warrants explanation. There is no native tracheal tissue presented for panels Figure 5k-n to compare.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting these important points regarding epithelial characterization and data integrity in Figure 5. Our detailed responses are as follows:
(1) Epithelial markers: KRT5/p63 vs. KRT14/ZO-1
We agree that KRT5 and p63 are widely used as basal cell markers in airway epithelium and provide critical information about progenitor cell identity. In our original submission, we primarily used KRT14 (CK14) and ZO-1 to assess epithelial coverage and barrier integrity, as KRT14 labels early epithelial progenitors and ZO-1 marks tight junction integrity. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have now performed additional IF staining for both KRT5 and p63 in regenerated tracheal epithelium from the BP-Gel+IL-Gel and BP-Gel groups, with native trachea as a reference. Based on a literature survey10,11, both KRT5 and p63 are standard basal markers, though KRT5 is more frequently applied for histological identification of airway structure, while p63 is often used in epithelial tumor classification. We therefore selected KRT5 as the basal marker and additionally included FOXJ1 as a marker of epithelial ciliary development.
Strong KRT5 and nuclear p63 expression were observed in the basal layers of regenerated epithelium in the BP-Gel+IL-Gel group, confirming the presence of basal progenitors and supporting pseudostratified epithelial restoration. Expression was sparse and discontinuous in the BP-Gel group (Fig. R1-7-1A; Fig. S12c in manuscript).
Figure R1-7-1 Regeneration of airway epithelium and cilia in trachea. (A-B) Representative fluorescence microscopy images of regenerated tracheal epithelium. KRT5 (red) and FOXJ1 (green) indicate basal progenitors and ciliated cells, while AC-Tub (green) marks mature cilia. (C) Quantification of epithelial cilia coverage confirms significant recovery in BP-Gel+IL-Gel compared with BP-Gel.
(2) Interpretation of KRT14 expression and potential squamous metaplasia?
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern that KRT14 (CK14) overexpression, particularly in multilayered formations, may suggest early squamous differentiation. To clarify, we performed additional co-staining analyses. IF staining for KRT5 and FOXJ1 confirmed the presence of basal progenitors and ciliated cells, while acetylated α-tubulin (AC-Tub) staining revealed abundant cilia formation in the BP-Gel+IL-Gel group but only minimal signals in the BP-Gel group (Fig. R1-7-1A-B; Fig. S12c in manuscript). Quantitative analysis of epithelial cilia coverage further demonstrated significant recovery in the BP-Gel+IL-Gel group (Fig. R1-7-1C; Fig. S12d in manuscript), indicating regeneration of a ciliated columnar epithelium rather than squamous metaplasia.
Although KRT14 overexpression has been linked to squamous differentiation, it is also widely recognized as a marker of early epithelial progenitors12-15. Combined with the evident ciliated phenotype, these results suggest that the KRT14-positive layer reflects active basal progenitor expansion and differentiation within an immune-supportive niche, rather than pathological squamous transformation.
(3) Explanation of differences in the replicate number across panels
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the variation in replicate numbers across panels. These differences reflect assay requirements and animal-use constraints. Physiological monitoring began with n = 8 rabbits per group, but numbers decreased over time due to survival differences. Histological analyses were conducted on three rabbits per group, with 6-10 random fields averaged per animal to avoid pseudoreplication. Mechanical testing was a destructive endpoint assay, and only three intact samples per group were available after allocating tissue for histology. Each reported n therefore represents independent animals, with technical replicates clearly distinguished. Despite these variations, results across survival, physiology, histology, and mechanics were consistent and statistically robust, supporting the validity of our conclusions.
Importantly, we have now revised the figure legend to explicitly state the rationale and exact replicate numbers for each panel.
(4) Inclusion of native trachea as control in Figure 5k-n
As requested, we have now included native rabbit trachea tissue sections stained for: H&E, AB&NFR, COL2A1 (IHC), KRT14+ZO-1 (IF). These are shown in Fig. R1-7-2 (Fig. 5k-n in manuscript). These serve as gold standard references for evaluating cartilage content and epithelial organization. Quantitative analyses, including cartilage area, COL2A1+ area, and epithelial thickness, have been updated and normalized to native tissue values where appropriate.
Figure R1-7-2 Histological and IF evaluation of cartilage and epithelial regeneration in trachea. (A) Quantitative analysis of the proportion of cartilage area in reconstructed trachea in different groups. (B-C) Representative COL2A1 IHC staining micrographs of reconstructed trachea harvested from different groups, and quantitative analysis of the ratio of COL2A1+ staining area. (D-E) Representative fluorescence microscopy images of epithelial tissues labeled with KRT14 (red) and ZO-1 (green) in different groups, and quantitative analysis of epithelial thickness. The dashed lines indicate the endothelial boundary.
We thank the reviewer for these valuable comments, which have significantly enhanced the rigor and clarity of our epithelial analysis.
8. Since inadequate perfusion represents a major barrier to successful long-segmental tracheal transplantation, the authors should clarify how reduced vessel formation in BOP-IL-Gel confers therapeutic benefit.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of vascularization in tissue-engineered constructs. We agree that adequate vascularization is essential for the survival of long-segment tracheal grafts. However, it is important to note that vascularization must occur in the correct tissue compartments. In our system, the reduced vascular infiltration within the cartilage core of the BP@IL-Gel group does not indicate perfusion deficiency but instead reflects a spatially selective anti-angiogenic effect that preserves cartilage integrity while supporting robust vascularization in the surrounding connective tissues.
In both native and engineered cartilage, excessive vascular ingrowth is detrimental, as it promotes chondrocyte apoptosis, matrix degradation, and pathological ossification or fibrotic remodeling16-18. In the BP-Gel group, histological and IF analyses showed marked vascular invasion into the cartilage rings, with upregulated MMP13 expression, reduced COL2A1 deposition, and increased α-SMA–positive vessel density in the cartilage core (Fig. R1-8-1A-E; Fig. 2q-t and 4j in manuscript). SO&FG staining further revealed a loss of proteoglycan-rich matrix, while ossification markers were elevated (Fig. R1-8-1F; Fig. S11i in manuscript). Together, these results demonstrate that uncontrolled angiogenesis within cartilage compromises structural stability and accelerates degeneration.
Figure R1-8-1 Evaluation of cartilage matrix integrity, degradation, and vascular invasion in BioC constructs. (A) Representative H&E-stained micrograph of BioC retaining a unilateral cortical layer. (B) Quantitative analysis of the invasion depth of surrounding tissues in BioC, comparing the side with cortical layer preservation (uncut) and the side without cortical layer preservation (cut). (C) IF staining micrograph showing the distribution of MMP13 (red) and COL2A1 (green) in BioC with a unilateral cortical layer. (D) Colocalization analysis of the MMP13 and COL2A1 distribution in BioC with a unilateral cortical layer. (E) Representative α-SMA (green) labeled fluorescence microscopy images of tissue specimens collected from different groups, and quantitative analysis of the number of blood vessels. The white triangles indicate the invasive blood vessels in cartilage tissue. (F) Representative SO&FG-stained micrographs of tissue specimens collected from the GelMA and GelMA@Blk groups and quantitative analysis of SO&FG-stained area. (G) Representative fluorescence microscopy images of tissue specimens labeled with PECAM1 (red) antibody in different groups. (H-I) Quantitative analysis of vascular area in the indicated regions.
By contrast, in the BP@IL-Gel group, IL-4/IL-13-induced M2 macrophage polarization effectively suppressed aberrant angiogenesis inside the cartilage while preserving the chondrocyte niche. PECAM1 immunostaining and quantitative analysis of vascular area revealed that vascularization was not diminished overall (Fig. R1-8-1G-I; Fig. S8m-o in manuscript). This selective vascular pattern closely mimics the zonal avascularity of native tracheal cartilage, where cartilage is nourished by diffusion from surrounding capillaries rather than by direct vascular penetration.
Further evaluation in the tracheal reconstruction model supported these findings. In the BP-Gel+IL-Gel group, H&E and α-SMA staining confirmed abundant, well-organized blood vessels between cartilage rings, comparable to native trachea, whereas the BP-Gel group displayed smaller, disorganized vessels (Fig. R1-8-2A; Fig. S12e in manuscript). Quantitative analysis demonstrated that vessel diameter and vascular area in the BP-Gel+IL-Gel group closely matched native trachea and were significantly greater than in the BP-Gel group (Fig. R1-8-2B; Fig. S12f in manuscript).
Figure R1-8-2 Vascularization in regenerated trachea. (A) Representative H&E and α-SMA IHC staining images of inter-cartilaginous tissues from the BP-Gel, BP-Gel+IL-Gel, and native groups. (B) Quantification of vascular diameter and mean vascular area.
Together, these results demonstrate that IL-Gel selectively modulates angiogenesis, suppressing pathological vessel ingrowth into the cartilage core while maintaining robust peripheral vascularization. This dual effect preserves cartilage integrity and matrix homeostasis while ensuring nutrient delivery, epithelial regeneration, and immune balance. In summary, BP@IL-Gel does not reduce overall perfusion but specifically prevents vascular invasion, which is critical for long-term structural stability and function. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion, which has greatly improved the clarity and rigor of our analysis.
9. Given that the major findings regarding enhanced chondrocyte functional and mechanical properties resulted from aggregate formation in BP+Gel conditions, the role of macrophage-mediated responses in this process requires further elucidation.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need to distinguish BP-Gel–driven aggregation from macrophage-mediated modulation. Our results support a two-step mechanism: BP-Gel creates the physical basis for chondrocyte aggregation and drives cartilage formation with mechanical and structural features close to native tissue, while IL-Gel-induced macrophage polarization further strengthens this newly formed cartilage and helps maintain its maturation, thereby enhancing chondrogenesis.
(1) Macrophage-mediated enhancement (in vitro)
In a transwell co-culture system, IL-Gel–polarized macrophages secreted elevated levels of trophic and angiocrine factors (TGF-β1, TGF-β3, IGF, bFGF, CCL2) after 7 days (Fig. R1-9-1A-B; Fig. 3e-f in manuscript). When chondrocytes in BP-Gel were co-cultured with these macrophages, toluidine blue staining revealed significant increases in both the number and area of cartilage matrix patches (Fig. R1-9-1C-E; Fig. 3g-i in manuscript), while IF confirmed higher COL2A1 expression with quantitative support (Fig. R1-9-1F-G; Fig. 3j-k in manuscript). In parallel, endothelial cells showed increased PECAM1 signals after 7 days of co-culture (Fig. R1-9-1H-I; Fig. 3l-m in manuscript), indicating macrophage-driven endothelial activation consistent with the establishment of a supportive perichondral niche.

(2) Macrophage-conditioned immune niche (in vivo)
In the reconstruction model, BP@IL-Gel established a more pro-chondrogenic immune niche than BP-Gel alone (Fig. R1-9-2A; Fig. 4b in manuscript). Histology revealed better preserved cartilage architecture (Fig. R1-9-2B; Fig. 4c in manuscript), with higher lacunae counts and increased hydroxyproline content (Fig. R1-18C-D; Fig. 4d-e in manuscript), consistent with enhanced matrix deposition and maturation under macrophage modulation.

(B) Representative H&E-stained micrographs of tissue specimens collected from different groups. (C) Quantitative analysis of the number of cartilage lacunae in different groups. (D) Quantitative analysis of hydroxyproline content in tissue specimens collected from different groups.
In line with our response in Comment 8, immunophenotyping showed that IL-Gel promoted macrophage polarization toward an M2 phenotype (MMR+/CD86−) in the perichondral region. This polarization correlated with reduced expression of inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, TNF-α) and decreased infiltration of α-SMA+ inflammatory vessels into the cartilage interior, while simultaneously maintaining robust vascularization in the peripheral connective tissue. Such vascular distribution ensures adequate nutrient delivery and supports epithelial regeneration, without disrupting the intrinsic avascularity of cartilage.
Together, these results indicate that while BP-Gel initiates chondrocyte aggregation, IL-Gel-polarized macrophages are pivotal in (i) supplying chondrogenic factors (TGF-β, IGF, bFGF), (ii) augmenting COL2A1-rich matrix formation, and (iii) activating endothelial cells to establish a vascularized perichondral rather than intra-cartilage niche. This macrophage-driven, spatially selective support preserves cartilage integrity and promotes functional tissue maturation in vivo. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion, which has helped us refine and strengthen our mechanistic interpretation.

Reviewer #3
This manuscript by Tang et al. presents a well-written and conceptually innovative study that introduces the Dynamic Tissue Engineering (DTE) strategy. This approach mimics embryonic cartilage development while concurrently modulating the immune microenvironment to support coordinated epithelial and vascular regeneration. The DTE strategy utilizes a bio-adaptive physical hydrogel (BP-Gel) in combination with an interleukin-loaded gel (IL-Gel), thereby enabling precise spatiotemporal control of the regenerative process. Meanwhile, the authors developed a new in vitro cell culture model and an in vivo tissue cultivation model, which together provide robust experimental support for the DTE approach. Moreover, the successful demonstration of tracheal reconstruction with favorable survival rates and functional outcomes underscores the translational potential of this strategy. Overall, the study is supported by the well-structured experimental design and comprehensive data, representing a meaningful advancement in tracheal tissue engineering.
Reply:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their encouraging and thoughtful comments. We are particularly grateful for the recognition of the conceptual innovation behind the Dynamic Tissue Engineering (DTE) strategy, as well as the translational significance of our findings. We have carefully addressed all detailed comments and concerns raised in the review, and we believe that the revised manuscript is now significantly improved in terms of scientific rigor, clarity, and reproducibility.
However, the following issues need to be further clarified and supplemented by the authors to enhance the overall rigor of the manuscript and ensure accurate communication of the study’s conclusions:
1. The authors introduced a novel paradigm for cartilage development and demonstrated its advantages over traditional cartilage culture under truly dynamic developmental conditions. However, the technical challenges associated with implementing this paradigm were not sufficiently elaborated. Compared to conventional methods, has there been any optimization in terms of culture duration or the required cell number? This should be detailed in the study.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this important point. Indeed, the Dynamic Tissue Engineering (DTE) strategy imposes specific technical challenges compared to static or pellet-based cartilage culture methods. We have now included a detailed explanation of these aspects in the revised manuscript.
(1) Technical challenges in the DTE paradigm
Unlike traditional pellet culture or scaffold-free pellet models, the DTE approach relies on cell-matrix remodeling within a soft, physically adaptive hydrogel, where cell aggregation, condensation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition occur in a 3D dynamic and mechanically evolving environment. The key technical challenges include: (a) Preserving chondrocyte viability while promoting cellular aggregation within a soft, shear-responsive hydrogel matrix that supports cell migration while preventing premature collapse; (b) Ensuring uniform cell seeding and homogeneous distribution in the hydrogel matrix; (c) Balancing gel mechanics by achieving stable gelation at 37℃ to maintain structural integrity during the initial stage, while allowing gradual degradation in synchrony with extracellular matrix deposition by chondrocytes at later stages. For instance, although Pluronic F127 also exhibits thermosensitive properties, its structural integrity only lasted for 48 h due to its rapid erosion in aqueous environments (Fig. R3-1-1; Fig. S3b in manuscript) and thus it is unable to support the full growth cycle of engineered cartilage.
Figure R3-1-1 Degradation comparison between Pluronic F127 and BP-Gel. Rose red was used to trace the F127-gel, while the BP-gel was highlighted with a blue background.
(2) Advantages over conventional cartilage culture approaches
Currently, the main approaches for bioengineered cartilage culture include: (a) pellet culture, in which high-density chondrocyte aggregation can generate small cartilage nodules, and some studies have further employed 3D printing of pellet units to construct larger cartilage tissues19 (Fig. R3-1-2A); (b) Another widely used and representative method is the in vitro culture of high-density chondrocytes. These cells can be stacked and shaped within molds20 (Fig. R3-1-2B), or seeded into pre-formed scaffolds, as employed in our previous study21 (Fig. R3-1-2C). Both approaches can be used to generate bioengineered cartilage.
Figure R3-1-2 Representative strategies for bioengineered cartilage culture. (A) Pellet culture and 3D-printed pellet assemblies. (B) High-density chondrocyte stacking in molds. (C) Seeding high-density chondrocytes onto pre-formed scaffolds.
However, these approaches lack the necessary cellular growth microenvironment and rely on cell stacking to promote cartilage development and ECM production. In contrast, during native cartilage development, intercellular signaling, mechanical cues, and heterogeneous oxygen distribution are critical for determining tissue-specific biological functions and microarchitectural organization. Compared with conventional cartilage tissue culture methods, the present study proposes an innovative strategy.
Moreover, conventional culture methods require a large number of chondrocytes, leading to increased costs and prolonged culture duration. In this study, we iterated on the above research. While conventional pellet culture requires a cell density of up to 2×108 cells/mL, and the cell density for high-density scaffold implantation is at least 3×107 cells/mL. Our study reduced the cell density to 4×106 cells/mL, a 7.5-50-fold reduction. With the optimization of the culture environment and the improvement of materials, the number of cells can be further reduced, which will enhance the application and translation potential of cartilage culture technology.
This information has now been added to the Materials and methods section:

Based on optimization experiments aimed at reducing chondrocyte usage while maintaining cartilage-forming capacity, the cell density was set at 4×106 cells/mL, which is substantially lower than used in traditional culture conditions, to enable the formation of BioC.”
In addition, we have revised the Discussion section and provided a more detailed elaboration on the relevant content:
Page 27, Line 6: “Macrolevel structural designs are insufficient to influence matrix fiber orientation or cortical organization, and thus fail to reproduce the spatiotemporal stress patterns that guide cartilage development. Therefore, current engineered cartilage tissues remain suboptimal in terms of its retention and development in vivo 22. Increasing evidence indicates that the native cartilage formation is closely related to its growth pattern and developmental stages23,24.”
Page 27, Line 24: “Meanwhile, within the BP-Gel, chondrocytes undergo aggregation and condensation at a significantly lower seeding density than required in conventional pellet cultures, while still supporting robust extracellular matrix deposition and cartilage-like tissue formation, thereby reducing cell consumption, minimizing culture costs, and enhancing translational potential.”

2. The authors mentioned that the physically crosslinked hydrogel exhibits a 3D polymer network that guides dynamic cell movement and promotes organized tissue development, which is a very novel and attractive finding. However, the background section does not clearly explain the detailed process of embryonic cartilage development. Clarifying the process of embryonic cartilage formation and highlighting both the similarities and differences between the cartilage development in BP-Gel and natural embryonic development is necessary to avoid reader confusion.
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion. We agree that the manuscript would benefit from a clearer explanation of embryonic cartilage development, particularly as it forms the biological rationale for our Dynamic Tissue Engineering (DTE) strategy.
First, we elaborate on the background of embryonic cartilage development in more detail.
Embryonic cartilage development is initiated through mesenchymal condensation, in which undifferentiated mesenchymal cells migrate, proliferate, and aggregate into dense clusters25. Within these condensations, cells commit to the chondrogenic lineage under the control of key transcription factors, most notably SOX926, and signaling pathways such as TGF-β, BMP, and Wnt/β-catenin27. These signals not only drive chondrocyte differentiation but also regulate extracellular matrix deposition, including type II collagen and proteoglycans, which form the structural framework of the cartilage primordium27. As development proceeds, the local microenvironment exerts profound influence25. Gradients of oxygen tension establish zonal heterogeneity, while mechanical cues derived from surrounding tissues guide matrix fiber orientation and stratified architecture28. The resulting “cortex-medulla” organization and anisotropic fiber alignment are essential for conferring mechanical resilience and load-bearing capacity29. Thus, the interplay between cellular signaling, biochemical regulation, and biophysical environment defines both the biological function and microstructure of native cartilage.
Based on this, we have revised the Introduction section and added a comprehensive description of embryonic cartilage development in the Discussion section, as follows:
Page 3, Line 14: “Specifically, the physical percolation network in the BP-Gel could dynamically adapt to the migration, proliferation, and aggregation of chondrocytes, thus facilitating the fusion of chondrocyte clusters into large aggregates. This procedure resembles the embryo-like chondrification process, in which undifferentiated mesenchymal cells migrate, proliferate, and condense to form cartilage primordia1-3.”
Page 27, Line 10: “During embryonic chondrogenesis, mesenchymal cells migrate, proliferate, and condense25, followed by differentiation into chondrocytes under the regulation of key transcription factors such as SOX926 and signaling pathways including TGF-β and Wnt/β-catenin27. These coordinated events give rise to the cartilage primordium and establish the basis for matrix deposition and structural organization27. Beyond molecular regulation, the local biophysical environment plays an equally critical role. Intercellular signaling, mechanical environment, and heterogeneous oxygen distribution are critical factors in determining the biological function and microstructure of cartilage3,30.”
Specifically, to illustrate the process of cartilage development more directly, we further performed histological staining (H&E, AB&NFR, and SO&FG) on mice embryonic trachea at E12.5, E14.5, and E16.5, stages that are characterized by initial mesenchymal condensation and the onset of cartilage matrix deposition. We observed that cells at the sites of tracheal cartilage development exhibited pronounced condensation in E12.5 embryos, while cartilage tissue gradually began to form at E14.5 and E16.5 (Fig. R3-2-1A; Fig. S6b in manuscript). In the in vitro cartilage culture using BP-Gel, chondrocytes also exhibited aggregation and fusion, whereas in the GelMA group, the cells remained consistently scattered throughout the culture period (Fig. R3-2-1B; Fig. S6a in manuscript). This comparison helps clarify that while our system does not fully replicate all embryonic morphogen gradients, it reconstructs key biophysical and organizational dynamics, particularly mesenchymal condensation, chondrocyte-driven ECM deposition, and zonal matrix structuring.
Figure R3-2-1 Chondrocyte condensation in embryonic trachea and in vitro cultures. (A) Mesenchymal condensation at E12.5 with cartilage formation at E14.5 and E16.5. (B) Representative histological images of chondrocytes cultured in BP-Gel and GelMA for 2 and 4 weeks in vitro.
We thank the reviewer again for raising this important point. By incorporating a mechanistic summary of embryonic cartilage development and drawing explicit parallels with our BP-Gel system, we believe the revised manuscript provides much clearer conceptual grounding for our DTE approach.
3. The observation of dynamic cellular aggregation in the results is quite exciting. This phenomenon is likely related to the physically crosslinked structure of the material itself. However, such behavior may be highly dependent on factors such as material concentration. Yet, the manuscript only use a single material concentration. What is the basis for this choice?
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the observed dynamic cellular aggregation is closely influenced by the physical properties of the BP-Gel matrix, which are in turn governed by its polymer concentration.
In our previous studies, thermosensitive hydrogel materials were generally applied at concentrations of approximately 25 wt% for biological applications, with further adjustments made depending on the desired degradation time and other parameters. Building on these prior experiences and the experimental data from the present study, we elected 12.5 wt% PLGA-PEG-PLGA as the working concentration for BP-Gel after preliminary screening of concentrations ranging from 6.5 to 25 wt%. Our results demonstrated that relatively low concentrations yielded hydrogels that were too soft to maintain structural integrity under culture conditions, leading to cell sedimentation and non-uniform distribution. In contrast, relatively high concentrations produced hydrogels with excessive stiffness and reduced porosity, which hindered chondrocyte migration and aggregation, resulting in scattered cells rather than functional condensates, similar to the distribution observed in GelMA (Fig. R3-3-1 A; Fig. S3a in manuscript). Moreover, using different cell types (macrophages and chondrocytes), we verified that the 12.5 wt% BP-Gel, upon gelation, exerted a low-adhesion effect on cells, which adopted a spherical morphology. Compared to conventional 2D culture plates, this environment promoted cellular aggregation and fusion (Fig. R3-3-1 B; Fig. S4c in manuscript).
Figure R3-3-1 Effects of BP-Gel concentration on hydrogel integrity and cell behavior. (A) Bright-field images of chondrocytes cultured in BP-Gel at different concentrations. (B) Morphology of macrophages and chondrocytes in 12.5 wt% BP-Gel compared with conventional 2D culture.
We thank the reviewer for prompting this clarification. By including the basis for concentration selection and new supporting data, we have strengthened the experimental rationale for our choice of BP-Gel formulation and its role in enabling dynamic cellular aggregation.
4. The BP-Gel system in this study is based on a thermosensitive PLGA-PEG-PLGA hydrogel, which undergoes a sol-gel transition near body temperature. However, the thermosensitive property does not appear to be prominently utilized or discussed as a functional feature in either in vitro or in vivo applications. The authors are encouraged to clarify whether thermosensitivity mainly serves as an operational convenience or whether it also contributes to cellular behavior modulation or tissue formation.
Reply:
We greatly appreciate this insightful comment, which indeed touches on a question we frequently consider as developers of biomaterials-namely, whether the intrinsic properties of a material can fully serve the requirements of its target application. We would like to address this from three perspectives.
First, the thermosensitivity of our system provides significant advantages that go beyond experimental convenience, directly contributing to the success of cartilage construction. For example, at room temperature, the system exhibits very low viscosity (G’＜1Pa), which allows chondrocytes to be homogeneously dispersed within the culture system. Upon warming to 37 ℃ (the standard cell culture temperature), the system rapidly solidifies without the need for any additional manipulation. Similarly, when constructing biomimetic connective tissue, the ability to cast IL-Gel at room temperature is not only convenient but also ensures complete filling of the inter-cartilage spaces due to its fluidity.
Second, we acknowledge that after the sol-gel phase transition (although this process is reversible), the subsequent cultivation and growth of engineered cartilage occur at 37 ℃, where the thermosensitive property per se does not directly influence cartilage growth. Nevertheless, we believe it is important to view material properties in an integrated rather than isolated manner, and I believe we can reach a consensus. As we have elaborated in the manuscript, the physical cross-linked network formed by PLGA-PEG-PLGA plays a vital role in supporting chondrocyte growth. The thermosensitivity, which inevitably arises from the amphiphilic micellar architecture of the polymer, was leveraged to optimize the cartilage engineering process, and we believe this represents a merit.
Finally, it should be noted that not all thermosensitive hydrogels are suitable for cartilage tissue engineering. For instance, although Pluronic F127 is also thermosensitive, it degrades completely within 72 h (Fig. R3-4-1; Fig. S3b in manuscript) and is thus unable to support the full growth cycle of engineered cartilage.
Figure R3-4-1 Degradation comparison between Pluronic F127 and BP-Gel. Rose red was used to trace the F127-gel, while the BP-gel was highlighted with a blue background.
We thank the reviewer again for the thoughtful suggestion. We have now clarified that thermosensitivity in the BP-Gel system plays both a practical and a biologically functional role in enabling dynamic tissue formation.

7. In Figs. 2e-f and Figs. S3e-g, the authors attempt to interpret cartilage condensation and development using the HIF-1α and YAP signaling pathways. Is this condensation process an essential step in native cartilage development? There is a lack of control data from natural cartilage, which should be supplemented to strengthen the explanation.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We would like to clarify that in Figs. 2e-f and S3e-g the interpretation was based on HIF-1α and COL2A1, rather than HIF-1α and YAP. Regarding the reviewer’s question, condensation is indeed an essential step in native cartilage development. During embryogenesis, undifferentiated mesenchymal cells aggregate into dense clusters, where transcription factors such as SOX9 and signaling pathways including TGF-β, BMP, and Wnt/β-catenin drive chondrocyte differentiation and matrix deposition. This process establishes the structural framework that, together with hypoxic and mechanical cues, gives rise to the “cortex-medulla” organization and anisotropic fiber alignment of functional cartilage.
As mentioned previously, to illustrate the process of cartilage development more directly, we further performed histological staining (H&E, AB&NFR, and SO&FG) on mice embryonic trachea at E12.5 stages that are characterized by initial mesenchymal condensation. We observed that cells at the sites of tracheal cartilage development exhibited pronounced condensation in E12.5 embryos (Fig. R3-7-1A; Fig. S6b in manuscript). In the in vitro cartilage culture using BP-Gel, chondrocytes also exhibited aggregation and fusion, whereas in the GelMA group, the cells remained consistently scattered throughout the culture period (Fig. R3-7-1B; Fig. S6a in manuscript). This comparison helps clarify that while our system does not fully replicate all embryonic morphogen gradients, it reconstructs key biophysical and organizational dynamics, particularly mesenchymal condensation, chondrocyte-driven ECM deposition, and zonal matrix structuring.
Figure R3-7-1 Chondrocyte condensation in embryonic trachea and in vitro cultures. (A) Mesenchymal condensation at E12.5. (B) Representative histological images of chondrocytes cultured in BP-Gel and GelMA for 2 and 4 weeks in vitro.
In our study, HIF-1α expression and COL2A1 deposition were used as readouts to capture microenvironmental influences on condensation and cartilage characteristics. We acknowledge that including native cartilage controls could provide additional reference; however, it is important to note that during the early condensation phase, mesenchymal stem cells drive cell clustering at a stage when chondrocyte-specific markers are not yet prominent, and characteristic cartilage genes such as COL2A1 only emerge at later stages of maturation. In our culture system, since chondrocytes were used as the starting population, the expression of HIF-1α and COL2A1 appeared at earlier stages.
Moreover, HIF-1α is the central transcription factor regulating cellular responses to hypoxia and plays a critical role in cartilage development. It is highly expressed in embryonic cartilage and growth plate cartilage, where it supports chondrocyte survival and differentiation under low-oxygen conditions. In mature cartilage, however, HIF-1α is maintained at a stable, low basal level, primarily to sustain metabolic homeostasis. Therefore, for the evaluation of HIF-1α and COL2A1 expression in this study, native tracheal cartilage does not serve as an entirely appropriate benchmark. Accordingly, we adopted a widely recognized model of chondrocyte development, namely the generation of cell spheroids, which form cartilage organoid-like aggregates. To further substantiate this point, we performed IF staining of HIF-1α and COL2A1 in cell spheroids (Fig. R3-7-2; Fig. 2e and S5c in manuscript). Consistent with developmental biology, HIF-1α was highly expressed during chondrogenic progression, accompanied by increased COL2A1 deposition. Notably, the distribution of HIF-1α differed between cell spheroids and BP-Gel constructs, which we attribute to environmental differences: BP-Gel constructs were partially surrounded by tissue, whereas cell spheroids were directly exposed to atmospheric oxygen, preventing stable retention of HIF-1α in the cytoplasm. Taken together, these results demonstrate that cartilage cultured within BP-Gel closely resembles cell spheroids, both exhibiting high expression of HIF-1α and COL2A1.
Figure R3-7-2 Fluorescence images of HIF-1α and COL2A1 in BP-Gel-cultured versus cell spheroids.
These results are now included in the Results section:
Page 8, Line 8: “Next, we explored the process of chondrocyte development in BioC. IF staining revealed that the expression of Collagen type II alpha 1 chain (COL2A1) and Hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) was significantly increased within the chondrocyte clusters formed in BP-Gel (Fig. 2e and S5a, showing an amplified region of Fig. 2e). Colocalization analysis based on protein expression intensity demonstrated that the expression levels of these two proteins were highly coincident (Fig. 2f and Fig. S5b). To further substantiate this point, we examined cell spheroids, a recognized model of chondrocyte development. IF staining showed high expression of HIF-1α and COL2A1 in cell spheroids, which closely resembled the expression patterns observed in BioC cultured within BP-Gel (Fig. S5c).”
We thank the reviewer for prompting this clarification and additional controls. By integrating native cartilage references, we believe the manuscript now provides stronger biological grounding during DTE-induced condensation.
8. In Fig. 4c, the presentation of cartilage development is relatively limited. It is necessary to include additional specific staining and biochemical assays of the cartilage matrix to better validate the promoting and protective effects of the BP@IL-Gel composite structure on ectopic cartilage development in vivo.
Reply:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion regarding the need for additional validation of cartilage matrix deposition and phenotype maintenance. We would like to clarify that these analyses were already included in our study. Specifically, after 2 weeks of in vivo implantation, H&E, AB&NFR, and COL2A1 IHC staining of the harvested tissues confirmed that the BP@IL-Gel composite exhibited the most pronounced cartilage-specific ECM deposition among the four groups (Fig. R3-8-1A; Fig. 4c and S11b-c in manuscript). Quantitative analysis of cartilage lacunae further demonstrated that the BP@IL-Gel group showed the highest number of lacunae (Fig. R3-8-1B; Fig. S11d in manuscript).
Figure R3-8-1 Histological staining and quantitative analysis of cartilage lacunae. (A) Representative H&E, AB&NFR and COL2A1 IHC staining micrographs of tissue specimens collected from different groups. (B) Quantitative analysis of the number of cartilage lacunae in different groups.
In addition, biochemical assays of cartilage matrix, including relative glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and hydroxyproline contents, revealed that the BP@IL-Gel structure design promoted both the maintenance of the cartilage phenotype and the protective effects on ectopic cartilage development (Fig. R3-8-2; Fig. S11e-f in manuscript).
Figure R3-8-2 Biochemical evaluation of cartilage matrix components. (A) Quantitative analysis of hydroxyproline content in tissue specimens collected from different groups. (B) Quantitative analysis of GAG content in tissue specimens collected from different groups.
We apologize if the original presentation did not sufficiently highlight these results, and we have now emphasized them more clearly in the revised manuscript. Accordingly, the corresponding results have been re-stated in the Results section to ensure clarity for readers:
Page 17, Line 29: “After 2 weeks of in vivo implantation, histological staining provided clear evidence of cartilage-specific matrix deposition. AB&NFR staining and COL2A1 IHC staining consistently showed that the BP@IL-Gel composite exhibited the most remarkable cartilage-specific ECM deposition among the four groups (Fig. 4c and S11b-d). To further quantify these observations, we analyzed cartilage lacunae based on the stained tissues and found that the number of lacunae was highest in the BP@IL-Gel group (Fig. 4d and S11d). In addition, biochemical assays of cartilage matrix demonstrated that relative glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and hydroxyproline contents were significantly elevated in the BP@IL-Gel group, indicating that this structural design effectively promoted maintenance of the cartilage phenotype and protected ectopic cartilage development (Fig. 4e and S11e-f).”
We thank the reviewer again for this constructive recommendation. The histological, immunohistochemical, and biochemical data substantiate the superior chondrogenic efficacy of the BP@IL-Gel composite.
9. In Fig. 4m, please clearly indicate which key genes related to the biological process are upregulated or downregulated, as this is critical for the interpretation of the sequencing results.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for emphasising the importance of distinguishing up‑ versus down‑regulated genes in the GO enrichment heat‑map (Fig. 4m). However, we would like to clarify that Fig. 4m in the manuscript (Fig. R3-9-1A) illustrates the correlation between biological processes and their associated molecular pathways. In this analysis, the ranking of each biological process is determined by the number of differentially expressed genes mapped to the corresponding pathway. Thus, the figure is primarily intended to reflect which pathways are most closely related to the observed alterations in local biological processes following treatment, rather than to indicate whether the associated pathways are up- or down-regulated.
Figure R3-9-1 GO enrichment and gene expression profiling of BP-Gel and BP@IL-Gel groups. (A) GO analysis of the RNA-seq data from the BP-Gel and BP@IL-Gel groups. (B) Relative expression of genes related to crucial processes, including inflammation and angiogenesis, in the BP-Gel and BP@IL-Gel groups.
Additionally, we evaluated the relative expression of genes associated with crucial processes, including inflammation and angiogenesis, in the BP-Gel and BP@IL-Gel groups (Fig. R3-9-1B; Fig. 4n in manuscript). Overall, the heat map allows us to roughly determine the expression trends of specific genes based on the color patterns. For instance, inflammation-related genes such as PTK2B, ALOX5, HMGB1, BTK, and HPSE exhibit an up-regulated trend. However, the sequencing results are presented here mainly to reflect the overall regulatory tendencies of the materials. The changes in individual genes are affected by many factors, and if the role of a specific gene in a biological process is to be elucidated, further investigation would be required. We will improve on this aspect in our subsequent studies, but it is not the primary focus of the present work.
We apologize for not having made this point sufficiently clear in the original version. We have now emphasized it more clearly in the revised manuscript. Accordingly, the corresponding results have been re-stated in the Results section to ensure clarity for readers:
Page 19, Line 7: “The analysis results indicate that BP@IL-Gel and BP-Gel exhibit distinct effects on modulating the inflammatory microenvironment and vascularization. The heat-map further allows a preliminary assessment of the up- or down-regulation trends of related genes (Fig. 4n).”
We hope this revision satisfies the reviewer’s request and improves the interpretability of our sequencing results. Thank you again for helping us strengthen the manuscript.
10. In Fig. 5, the authors suggest that IL-Gel can protect cartilage from vascular invasion. Does IL-Gel hinder capillary regeneration around the cartilage? This needs to be addressed in the manuscript, with additional data provided if necessary.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. We would like to emphasize that the protective effect of IL-Gel on cartilage is not achieved by indiscriminate inhibition of angiogenesis. Instead, IL-Gel reshapes the inflammatory microenvironment, selectively preventing pathological vascular invasion into cartilage while supporting the regeneration of functional capillaries in the surrounding tissue. This distinction is critical for maintaining the avascularity required for hyaline cartilage maturation, without compromising peripheral perfusion that provides nutrients and immune regulation.
(1) IL-Gel promotes organized peripheral angiogenesis
IF staining for PECAM1 demonstrated that blood vessels in the IL-Gel group were more abundant, evenly distributed, and structurally organized compared with BP-Gel alone (Fig. R3-10-1A; Fig. S8m in manuscript). Quantitative analysis further confirmed a significantly greater vascular area in the perichondral regions of IL-Gel constructs, comparable to native controls (Fig. R3-10-1B-C; Fig. S8n-o in manuscript). These findings indicate that IL-Gel facilitates functional angiogenesis around cartilage tissue.
Figure R3-10-1 IL-Gel promotes functional and organized angiogenesis in vivo. (A) Representative fluorescence microscopy images of tissue specimens labeled with PECAM1 (red) antibody in different groups. (B-C) Quantitative analysis of vascular area in the indicated regions.
(2) IL-Gel prevents pathological vascular invasion into cartilage
In contrast, α-SMA staining showed that in the BP-Gel group, inflammation-driven vessels penetrated the cartilage core, correlating with accelerated matrix degradation and ossification. SO&FG staining revealed a concomitant reduction in proteoglycan-rich cartilage area (Fig. R3-10-2; Fig. 4j and S11i in manuscript). By comparison, IL-Gel treatment suppressed aberrant intra-cartilage vascularization, thereby preserving cartilage lacunar structure and matrix integrity.
Figure R3-10-2 IL-Gel prevents aberrant vascular invasion and preserves cartilage integrity. (A) Representative α-SMA (green) labeled fluorescence microscopy images of tissue specimens collected from different groups, and quantitative analysis of the number of blood vessels. The white triangles indicate the invasive blood vessels in cartilage tissue. (B) Representative SO&FG-stained micrographs of tissue specimens collected from the GelMA and GelMA@Blk groups and quantitative analysis of SO&FG-stained area.
(3) IL-Gel exhibits intrinsic pro-angiogenic capacity in vitro
To further evaluate its angiogenic potential, we examined endothelial responses in vitro. IL-Gel-induced macrophage polarization significantly enhanced HUVEC migration, tube formation, and the expression of endothelial cell-related genes (PECAM1, VEGF) compared with controls (Fig. R3-10-3; Fig. 3l-m and S10c-f in manuscript). These results demonstrate that IL-Gel not only permits but actively promotes angiogenesis under controlled conditions.
Figure R3-10-3 Pro-angiogenic effects of IL-Gel on HUVEC migration, tube formation, and gene expression. (A-B) Representative fluorescence microscopy images and quantitative analysis of endothelial cells labeled with PECAM1 (red) after 7 days of culture in the co-culture system. (C) Expression levels of endothelial cell-related genes (PECAM1 and VEGFA) in HUVECs cultured in the co-culture system for 7 days. (D-E) Representative images and quantitative analysis of endothelial cell migration in different groups. (F) Representative images and quantitative analysis of endothelial cell tube formation in different groups.
In summary, IL-Gel does not hinder capillary regeneration. Instead, it promotes well-organized vascularization in the perichondral niche while preventing destructive vascular ingrowth into cartilage tissue. This dual effect creates a balanced microenvironment that simultaneously preserves cartilage avascularity and structural integrity, while ensuring sufficient nutrient delivery and epithelial support. Therefore, we have highlighted this clarification in the revised manuscript, specifically in the Results section:
Page 14, Line 7: “The IL-Gel group exhibited more functional blood vessels with an orderly arrangement (Fig. S8m-o). These findings suggest that IL-Gel promotes endothelial cell growth.”
Page 15, Line 8: “Moreover, scratch assays and tube formation assays discovered that the presence of IL-Gel substantially boosted the migratory ability of HUVECs (Fig. S10d-e) and promoted angiogenesis (Fig. S10f). These results suggest that IL-Gel facilitates well-organized angiogenesis.”
Page 18, Line 24: “Moreover, the increased vascular infiltration in the BP-Gel group made the cartilage more susceptible to ossification, as evidenced by SO&FG staining (Fig. S11i). Collectively, these results suggest that IL-Gel facilitates well-organized angiogenesis while avoiding aberrant vascular infiltration into cartilage tissue.”
In addition, we have incorporated the following statement in the Discussion section:
Page 27, Line 30: “In addition to the intrinsic growth and developmental status of cartilage, extrinsic environmental factors also play a critical role in determining its long-term persistence in vivo. Cartilage development requires a relatively low-metabolic niche, and excessive vascular invasion can accelerate cartilage degradation. The beneficial effect of IL-Gel arises not from a direct inhibition of angiogenesis, but from reshaping the inflammatory microenvironment to prevent pathological vascular overgrowth into cartilage. Meanwhile, IL-Gel promotes functional vascularization in the surrounding tissue, ensuring adequate nutrient supply without compromising cartilage integrity.”
We thank the reviewer for this important comment, which has greatly assisted us in refining the presentation and clarifying the key points of our study.
11. In Figs. 5b-c, the authors report average values of survival and respiratory function in rabbits after orthotopic tracheal transplantation. Please provide detailed individual data for each animal model to improve data transparency.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of data transparency, particularly in preclinical animal studies. We agree that providing the individual values for survival and respiratory function enhances the reproducibility and credibility of the findings. We have now included detailed animal data for each group in a newly added Table S3.
We appreciate the reviewer’s recommendation. The individual animal data are now included as Supplementary Table S3, ensuring full transparency and reproducibility of our tracheal transplantation findings.
12. Please supplement the vascular-specific staining (e.g., CD31) of the orthotopic graft sections and include quantitative analysis, as vascularization is also crucial for tracheal regeneration.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion regarding vascularization in the orthotopic grafts. In response, we have now supplemented vascular-specific staining and quantitative analyses of the regenerated trachea.
Instead of PECAM1 (CD31), we selected α-SMA as the primary marker to characterize vascular distribution in the grafts. The rationale is that the orthotopic grafts were harvested at relatively late stages of regeneration, by which time many vessels had already matured. While PECAM1 is well-suited for identifying newly formed endothelial cells and nascent capillaries31, α-SMA highlights mature, stabilized vessels with perivascular smooth muscle coverage32, which more accurately reflect long-term perfusion capacity and functional integration of the graft. Moreover, α-SMA staining allows clear visualization of vessel wall structure, enabling robust morphometric measurements of vascular diameter and wall thickness33. Thus, α-SMA provides a reliable representation of the functional vasculature necessary for sustained graft survival.
Our staining results confirmed the presence of abundant vessels between the cartilage rings in the experimental group (BP-Gel+IL-Gel). Quantitative analysis demonstrated that both vessel diameter and vascular area were comparable to those observed in native trachea, indicating well-established and functional perfusion. By contrast, the BP-Gel only group also exhibited increased vascular density; however, these vessels were significantly smaller in caliber and irregularly distributed, consistent with disorganized neovascularization likely driven by inflammation rather than functional remodeling (Fig. R3-12-1; Fig. S12e-f in manuscript).
Figure R3-12-1 Vascularization in regenerated trachea. (A) Representative H&E and α-SMA IHC staining images of inter-cartilaginous tissues from the BP-Gel, BP-Gel+IL-Gel, and native groups. (B) Quantification of vascular diameter and mean vascular area.
Taken together, these findings demonstrate that IL-Gel not only preserves cartilage integrity but also supports the development of mature, functional vasculature in the perichondral regions of orthotopic grafts, thereby ensuring adequate nutrient supply and promoting long-term tracheal regeneration. We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. The added vascular staining and quantification further demonstrate the functional integration and regenerative competence of our engineered tracheal grafts.
13. What is the difference between the results of Fig. S7 and Fig. 3f? Please further clarify their respective significance.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. Indeed, both Fig. 3f and Fig. S7 (Now Fig. S10 in manuscript) are central to demonstrating the role of IL-Gel in activating macrophage polarization and subsequently influencing chondrocyte and endothelial development. These two figures represent two complementary but distinct models within our study.
Fig. S7 (Now Fig. S10 in manuscript) reflects the direct effects of IL-Gel on macrophages, highlighting their polarization status and cytokine secretion profile. This model is essential for confirming that IL-4/13-loaded IL-Gel can effectively drive macrophages toward an M2 phenotype.
However, Fig. 3f presents the functional consequences of macrophage polarization, focusing on how IL-Gel-induced M2 macrophages influence downstream cell types, including chondrocytes, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells. Specifically, Fig. S7 (Now Fig. S10 in manuscript) shows enhanced gene expression, migration, tube formation, and chondrogenic/angiogenic potential of these target cells under co-culture with polarized macrophages.
Taken together, Fig. 3f and Fig. S7 (Now Fig. S10 in manuscript) provide two layers of evidence: one at the level of macrophage polarization itself, and the other at the level of its impact on surrounding structural and vascular cells. This integrated approach highlights the mechanistic cascade by which IL-Gel reshapes the immune microenvironment to promote cartilage and vascular development.
Correspondingly, we have revised the Results section to include these findings:
Page 14, Line 14: “We first established a co-culture system to examine the direct effects of IL-Gel on macrophage polarization, thereby confirming the ability of IL-4/13-loaded IL-Gel. We quantified cytokine levels in the culture medium of macrophages subjected to different treatments, as illustrated in Fig. S10a.”
Page 14, Line 22: “To mimic the in vivo microenvironment, building upon this, we further established a co-culture system to co-culture macrophages with chondrocytes, endothelial cells, or epithelial cells (Fig. 3f). The results illustrate the functional consequences of IL-Gel-induced macrophage polarization, demonstrating how polarized macrophages subsequently regulate the growth and development of chondrocytes, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells.”
We thank the reviewer again for prompting this clarification. By clearly distinguishing the experimental context and purpose of these two figures, we ensure accurate interpretation of the immune regulatory dynamics at different phases and model systems.
14. In the Materials and Methods section, some experimental descriptions are relatively vague, which affects reproducibility. Please provide more detailed parameters and protocols for each experimental procedure.
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s emphasis on the importance of methodological clarity. We have now systematically revised the Materials and Methods section to ensure full reproducibility and transparency. All modifications are clearly marked in the revised manuscript using the Word track-changes mode for ease of review. We have carefully revised the Methods section to meet high standards of experimental reproducibility. We believe these additions will facilitate future replication and enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
